# Semantic Validation with LLMs {#sec-semantic-validation}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```


Some expectations are hard to write as code. Whether a product review is a real, on-topic comment
is a judgment about meaning, and no regular expression or set membership check can make it. The
`prompt()` method handles cases like this. It sends each row to a language model along with a plain
description of what a good row looks like, and turns the model's answer into an ordinary pass or
fail test unit that appears in the report next to your other checks.

This comes with costs that regular checks do not have. Each check costs money, takes much longer to
run, and may not give exactly the same answer twice. So semantic validation is something to use on
purpose, not by default. This chapter covers how the method works, how to write prompts that give
reliable answers, how to include reference material as attachments, how to manage the cost, and how
the results fit into the rest of a validation plan. We use a small table of product reviews for the
examples.

```{python}
reviews = pl.DataFrame({
    "review_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "product": ["wireless mouse", "desk lamp", "coffee mug", "usb cable"],
    "review_text": [
        "Works great, very responsive and comfortable to use all day.",
        "asdkjfh lorem ipsum dolor sit amet",
        "The lamp is bright and the base is sturdy. Very happy with it.",
        "n/a",
    ],
})

pb.preview(reviews, n_head=4, n_tail=0)
```

Reviews 1 and 3 are real comments about a product, while reviews 2 and 4 are junk. A length check
would catch `"n/a"`, but not the keyboard mash and placeholder text in review 2, which is 34
characters long. This is the kind of situation semantic validation is for.

## How `prompt()` works

The `prompt()` method takes a plain-language description of what makes a row valid and the name of
a model, and asks the model to judge each row against that description. Each row is a test unit that
passes or fails, and the results show up in the report like any other check. The `columns_subset=`
argument limits which columns are sent to the model, which keeps the model focused and avoids
sending data it does not need.

```{python}
#| eval: false
(
    pb.Validate(data=reviews)
    .prompt(
        prompt="The review_text should be a coherent, on-topic comment about the product.",
        columns_subset=["product", "review_text"],
        model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

The model name has the form `provider:model`. The supported providers are `"anthropic"`,
`"openai"`, `"ollama"`, `"bedrock"`, and `"azure-openai"`, and the part after the colon is the
specific model. You never pass an API key as an argument. Pointblank reads it from an environment
variable or from a `.env` file in your project, so an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`
variable is picked up automatically. Ollama runs models on your own machine and needs no key. Rows
are sent to the model in batches (1,000 rows per batch by default, set with `batch_size=`), but each
row still gets its own result. For this table, you would expect reviews 1 and 3 to pass and reviews
2 and 4 to fail.

## Multimodal attachments

Sometimes the standard depends on reference material that is hard to put into words, such as a
brand style guide or a diagram. The `attachments=` argument accepts images (`.png`, `.jpg`,
`.jpeg`, `.gif`, and `.webp`) and PDFs, and sends them to the model as context that applies to every
row. Each row's own values are still sent as data.

```{python}
#| eval: false
(
    pb.Validate(data=reviews)
    .prompt(
        prompt="The review_text should match the tone and vocabulary in the attached brand guide.",
        columns_subset=["product", "review_text"],
        attachments=["docs/brand_guide.pdf"],
        model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5",
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

With the attachment, the model can compare each review against the guide without the guide's rules
having to be written into the prompt. Attachments do add cost, though, because an attachment is sent
again with every batch. A table big enough to need several batches pays for the attachment several
times. To keep this down, keep attachments small (for example, by shrinking an image or cutting a
PDF down to the pages that matter) and fit more rows into each batch.
